The horizontal nystagmus on Dix–Hallpike may reflect “cross-coupling” or atypical response, but is more commonly seen in horizontal canal BPPV — especially if also confirmed on supine roll test.

[SUMMARY]  
**Diagnosis:**  
✅ **Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), right-sided** — confirmed by history and positive Dix–Hallpike maneuver.  

**Key Supporting Findings:**  
- Vertigo: Brief (<60 sec), latency (~1–10 sec), provoked by head position changes (rolling over, bending, looking up).

**Clinical Recommendation:**

➡️ Avoid Epley maneuver unless posterior canal BPPV is confirmed (e.g., torsional-upbeating nystagmus on Dix–Hallpike).  

**Prognosis & Counseling:**  
- Excellent prognosis with appropriate repositioning: >90% resolution within 1–3 treatments.  
- Recurrence rate ~30–50% at 5 years; reassurance and home balance exercises may be offered.  
- No further workup (MRI, audiometry) indicated in absence of atypical features.

The case is definitively BPPV — no diagnostic ambiguity remains. No other condition explains this precise constellation: vestibular neuritis lacks positional triggering and shows spontaneous nystagmus; Menière’s includes cochlear symptoms; CNS lesions cause persistent or non-positional symptoms and lack fatigable nystagmus.
